source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Preregistered test of 37 prompts against a control on 100 ForecastBench questions and 4 models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Llama 3.1 405B). Most prompts did nothing. Base-rate prompts were among the few that helped a little.
numbers: One-sample t-tests, Brier difference vs control: Frequency-Based Reasoning -0.019 (N=370, BH adj p=0.022), Base Rate First -0.016 (N=390, adj p=0.036), Step-Back -0.015 (N=391, adj p=0.036). Bayesian Reasoning and Propose-Evaluate-Select were significantly worse (PES +0.028, N=391, p<0.001).
limits: Effect is small (about 0.01 to 0.02 Brier). In the preregistered mixed-effects model (random intercepts for question and model) no prompt beat control after correction: Base Rate First -0.011, adj p=0.774.
agent_relevance: A base-rate-first instruction is cheap and probably slightly positive, but it is not a large lever. Do not expect S0 alone to move Brier by more than about 0.01 to 0.02.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: The Multiple Reference Classes prompt did not help. Asking for several comparison classes was no better than control.
numbers: Mixed model: -0.004 (z=-0.82, adj p=0.774). One-sample t-test: p=0.113, adj p=0.233, N=391.
limits: Single study, 100 questions, one control prompt. Underpowered for effects of 0.005.
agent_relevance: Naming one good class may beat listing many. If the agent lists several classes it needs a rule to pick or combine them.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Study 2 combined the best prompts and compared them with developer prompts and literature prompts, adding o1 and o1-mini. No combined prompt robustly beat the control.
numbers: Base Rate First + Frequency-Based -0.012 (SD 0.144, N=462, p=0.072, adj p=0.162); Base Rate First + Chain of Thought -0.007 (p=0.212); Mandatory Probability + Base Rate Fallback -0.002 (p=0.716).
limits: The Study 1 gains did not replicate inside the same paper when combined. Study 1 effects may be noise from 38 prompts.
agent_relevance: Treat the base-rate prompt effect as unreplicated. Gains may come from tools and retrieval, not from the wording of the comparison-class instruction.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Prompts changed how decisive forecasts were. Reasoning prompts pushed forecasts away from 50%. Base Rate First stayed moderate.
numbers: Mean absolute distance from 0.5: Bayesian Reasoning 0.199, Chain of Thought 0.172, Base Rate First 0.159, Multiple Reference Classes 0.139; control and Anti-Biasing (Anchoring) about 0.119 to 0.134.
limits: Distance from midpoint is not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Base-rate prompting did not add much overconfidence.

source: Pratt, Blumberg, Carolino, Morris (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
finding: PaLM 2 chained-prompt forecasters using human-forecasting strategies (breakdown, base rates, both sides, crowd, news) on 351 validation events. None beat the plain just-answer baseline on Brier.
numbers: Brier (validation): Human 0.1334, Basic 0.1221, Forecaster-prompt 0.1483, Breakdown 0.1895, Base Rates 0.1562, Both Sides 0.1553, Crowd 0.1706, News API 0.1235. Base-rate strategy was 0.034 worse than basic.
limits: One model (PaLM 2), one dataset (Glean prediction-market events, mostly resolving No). The test set (341 events) showed the same pattern.
agent_relevance: On a dataset where most events resolve No, a base-rate step that raises the probability hurts. Check the class frequency before anchoring.

source: Pratt, Blumberg, Carolino, Morris (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
finding: The authors explain this by a negativity bias: the plain prompt gave low probabilities, which paid off because most events resolved No. Asking for a rationale raised probabilities. Weighting Yes and No events equally flipped the ranking.
numbers: Weighted Brier: Human 0.1746, Basic 0.1955, Forecaster 0.2097, Breakdown 0.2053, Base Rates 0.2540, Both Sides 0.2159, Crowd 0.1860, News 0.1950. Base-rate strategy worst when weighted.
limits: Weighted Brier is the authors' own post-hoc metric. Event mix is dataset specific.
agent_relevance: A low-prior bias can look like good outside-view reasoning. Test on balanced question sets so base-rate use is not confused with a No bias.

source: Pratt, Blumberg, Carolino, Morris (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
finding: The base-rate module asked the model to state a base rate from memory, then adjust. The self-generated base rate was a weak anchor.
numbers: Base Rates Brier 0.1562 vs Basic 0.1221 (validation).
limits: Pipeline used model-recalled base rates with no data lookup.
agent_relevance: If the agent only recalls a class frequency from memory it can be wrong. Prefer retrieved or computed frequencies.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Retrieval-augmented GPT-4 system whose scratchpad ends by asking the model to check for over- or under-confidence and to consider historical base rates. Nears the human crowd.
numbers: Test Brier 0.179 (system) vs 0.149 (crowd); accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Random baseline 0.250. Ablation table (crowd 0.146): base GPT-4 with retrieval about 0.181; without retrieval 0.183 in one row; neither retrieval nor fine-tuned reasoning 0.206.
limits: The base-rate line is one part of a multi-step prompt and was not ablated alone. Questions from 5 platforms; hyperparameters tuned on validation.
agent_relevance: Shows the base-rate check as a late calibration step after arguments, while our S0 puts it first. The two orders have not been compared head to head.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: The system beats the crowd only where the crowd is uncertain.
numbers: When crowd predictions are between 0.3 and 0.7: system Brier 0.199 vs crowd 0.246. On one condition covering 84% of forecasts: system 0.175 vs crowd 0.143.
limits: Subsetting was chosen after seeing model strengths.
agent_relevance: Where the class frequency is lopsided the crowd or a base rate is already strong. Models add value where the case is close to 50%.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Zero-shot prompting of 14 LMs without retrieval is near chance. Prompt choice matters at zero-shot.
numbers: Best zero-shot prompt mean Brier 0.246 across 14 LMs; other candidate prompts 0.252, 0.261, 0.276, 0.279. Random baseline 0.250.
limits: Averaged over 14 models, many weak.
agent_relevance: Raw models do not apply comparison classes by themselves. A scaffold must force it.

source: Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters (2025)
finding: Scoring caveat: Brier scores are not comparable across questions with different base rates, and calibration can reward a pure base-rate forecaster.
numbers: A forecaster who always gives the true base rate b has expected Brier b(1-b). Example: 50 questions at 50% plus 50 at 5%; perfect on rare ones but baseline on coin flips gives about 0.125; clueless on rare ones but 0.25 to 0.15 on coin flips gives about 0.10. Cardinal example: 1% to all 100 cardinals is perfectly calibrated.
limits: Mathematical argument plus examples, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Score S0 against a per-class base-rate forecaster, not raw Brier. Otherwise class frequency looks like skill.

source: Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters (2025)
finding: Shortcut check: a small 2021 DeBERTa model fine-tuned on question text only, no retrieval, predicts outcomes well above chance on generated sets. Some benchmarks reward priors in the wording.
numbers: Accuracy up to 80% on a four-choice generated MCQ set (chance 25%); 55% after re-running the pipeline with DeepSeek v3 0324; Metaculus 55% and Manifold 59% (binary).
limits: Real-platform binary sets are close to chance, so shortcut is small there.
agent_relevance: Use real resolved platform questions to test an outside-view step.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Superforecasters beat the best LLM. The best LLMs had the crowd price in the prompt; without it the best model was worse.
numbers: 200-question subset: superforecasters 0.096, public 0.121, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.122, best model without market crowd 0.136. On a separate dataset-questions split: superforecasters 0.076, public 0.096, GPT-4o 0.130 (gap 0.054 vs 0.026 between GPT-4o and GPT-4).
limits: Freeze values means the current market value or last data point is given to the model. That is a status-quo anchor, not a reference class.
agent_relevance: The strongest anchor LLMs use is the current value. S0 can treat current value as a class of one.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: A benchmark prompt makes reference class and base rate the second step, then asks for reasons above and below the base rate. It falls back to the base rate if the model cannot answer.
numbers: Prompt text: pick the base rate, but return a number between 0 and 1; base rate should be as specific as it's possible to be without losing confidence that the number is correct.
limits: The paper reports results per model and prompt condition but no ablation of the base-rate step alone.
agent_relevance: A ready template for S0: pick class, state number, justify, then list reasons up and down. The narrow-the-class rule is useful.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: A twelve-LLM crowd, prompted to start from reference or comparison classes and base rates, matches a human crowd of 925 on 31 questions. Individual models leaned above 50%.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.85. Individual models: GPT-4 0.15, Claude 2 0.21, Llama-2-70B 0.25, Coral 0.38. Mean forecast 57.35% vs 14 of 31 resolving Yes.
limits: 31 questions only. The prompt had many elements, so the base-rate part is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Median over models cancels the above-50% bias. A class anchor and a crowd step may be partly redundant.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd: LLM Ensemble Prediction Capabilities Rival Human Crowd Accuracy
finding: Showing the model the human median improved it, but averaging model and human did better.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 (p=0.003); Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 (p<0.001); accuracy gain 17% to 28%.
limits: Study 2 only.
agent_relevance: External anchors work. S0 should accept a given crowd or market number as the anchor when one exists, then adjust.

source: Schoenegger and Park (2023) Large Language Model Prediction Capabilities: Evidence from a Real-World Forecasting Tournament
finding: GPT-4 with a superforecaster prompt that told it to use base rates did no better than predicting 50% on a Metaculus tournament.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier 0.20 (SD 0.18) vs human crowd 0.07 (SD 0.08); vs 0.25 baseline t(22)=-1.23, p=0.23.
limits: Small N (23 questions in the test); the prompt had many parts, so the base-rate effect is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Base-rate wording alone was not enough in 2023. Later work added retrieval and ensembling.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Used the reference-class idea to build test data. An LLM changes key entities in a news-derived question to make sibling questions in the same class, which reduces the bias that article-derived questions resolve Yes.
numbers: 2,621 ground-truth-resolved questions from NewsAPI (July 1 to Aug 21 2024); ground-truth label error under 5% in their tests; 242 of 500+ platform questions passed verification.
limits: Used for data building, not for the forecaster's own reasoning.
agent_relevance: The agent could do the same: generate sibling cases to estimate class frequency, then test whether the case differs.

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting
finding: A ReAct agent whose first planned step is Reference Classes and Base Rates uses Python to count how often an asset closed above a level, then adjusts. It matches the crowd.
numbers: RTF Brier 0.169 (median of 3), 0.170 (mean) vs Manifold crowd 0.172; sampled single run 0.180; GPT-4o 0.210; Halawi et al. GPT-4o 0.177; base LM ensemble 0.218. Worked example: ETH above 3700, 80 of 1003 days gives 8%; another run used 30%.
limits: Small set of Manifold questions; base-rate step not ablated alone. Different runs picked different classes (30% vs 8%).
agent_relevance: Outside view as a computed number via a tool. The 30% vs 8% spread shows S0 needs a stated class and a count.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Technical Report
finding: Agentic search forecaster. A supervisor that sees several forecasters' traces issues search queries, often to look up a base rate or fact-check. Market prices help, but the price alone beats a prior LLM system.
numbers: Market price only 0.096 vs best prior LLM 0.109 on the same subset; AIA 0.075 with search and price, 0.085 with search and no price; no-search 0.116 (0.103 with price). Price closes 42% of the gap. ForecastBench: no search 0.1230, best agentic search 0.1140.
limits: Technical report, not peer reviewed. Market prices are a crowd outside view.
agent_relevance: Base-rate lookup is used as a reconciliation step after disagreement, not only at the start. A second S0-style pass when drafts disagree is plausible.

source: FutureSearch (2025) Bench to the Future: A Pastcasting Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
finding: Agent prompt gives explicit outside-view rules: use base rates for similar past events, put more weight on the inside view when events are unique, favour the status quo. Snapshots of about 20,000 pages per question include multiple base rates.
numbers: Example: base rate is a good start for Will the temperature in Miami exceed 100 degrees next month. About 20,000 pages crawled per question.
limits: Prompt design only; the paper compares models, not these lines.
agent_relevance: Gives wording for when to down-weight the class: unique events need the inside view.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in Large Language Models
finding: Across three LLMs, judgment biases (base-rate, anchoring, sunk cost, status quo) show a 19.8% bias rate on Malberg30k, and a debiasing prompt made accuracy worse.
numbers: Prompt-level debiasing: Judgment accuracy -4.4% (backfires), Info Processing -1.1%, Social +5.9%, Response position independence +40.5%. Activation steering cut bias score 26% to 32%.
limits: Pooled over four judgment categories; base-rate alone not reported in the text I read. Preprint under review.
agent_relevance: A generic be-unbiased line will not fix base-rate neglect. Use a concrete procedure: name class, get number.

source: Mu et al. (2025) Who is More Bayesian: Humans or ChatGPT?
finding: In the cage-and-balls task (given prior plus sample), GPT-3.5 often ignored the prior, GPT-4 knew Bayes rule but made algebra errors, and GPT-4o was near perfect.
numbers: Decision efficiency vs humans: GPT-3.5 12.1% lower (Wisconsin) and 21.9% lower (Holt-Smith); GPT-4 comparable; GPT-4o 1% and 3.5% higher; o1 near 100%. GPT-3.5 average accuracy 59.4%; GPT-4 77.7% (6-ball). Human efficiency 92.5% to 96%.
limits: Textbook urn task with the prior given; no need to find a class.
agent_relevance: Combining a given prior with evidence is solved by recent models. The hard part is choosing the class and number.

source: Scholten et al. (2024) Metacognitive Myopia in Large Language Models
finding: Argues LLMs show a base-rate-neglect symptom: they condition on the prompt sample and do not track missing cases or the true population frequency. Asking for popular artists leans to pop.
numbers: Conceptual paper; no accuracy numbers for this symptom.
limits: Theory with examples, no experiment on base rates.
agent_relevance: Mechanism for why the class must be named from outside the prompt.

source: Suri et al. (2023) Do Large Language Models Show Decision Heuristics Similar to Humans? A Case Study Using GPT-3.5
finding: GPT-3.5 was swayed by salient case information over base-rate information in representativeness and availability tasks, as humans are.
numbers: Qualitative statement in the discussion; exact rates not extracted.
limits: Preliminary, one model. The Linda problem itself was evaded, so the authors built a similar one.
agent_relevance: The pull of the vivid case is real. Present the class before the case details.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs
finding: Related-work remark: earlier tests of representativeness and base-rate neglect in LLMs were one-off questions, which limits generalization.
numbers: Cites Talboy and Fuller (2023). No base-rate numbers in this paper.
limits: Only a related-work remark.
agent_relevance: Do not trust one-item demos of base-rate neglect. Use many items with ground truth.
